body.statement:
Under the formal specialization of the displayed constructions to \(m=1\), one has \(B=A\) and \(Q=D\). Consequently, \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) is empty when \((B,Q)\) violates any fine-grid compatibility constraint and otherwise equals the singleton \(\{(B,Q)\}\). Accordingly, on an admissible exact input the certificate returns incompatibility in the first case, while in the second case it returns the unique transfer
\[
h_{uv}(z)=\frac{B_{vu}z}{1-B_{vv}z},
\]
which is the standard unaliased direct process transfer.
body.justification: This verifies that the new machinery collapses to the familiar fine-grid formula when aliasing is removed.
body.gap: The reduction is not a novelty claim; it is the required fidelity check against standard process-graph transfer analysis.
body.consumer: Implementers can test the certificate against an unaliased benchmark before using it on subsampled data.
body.proof_tex:
Formally specialize Definition~\texttt{def:compatible-fiber} and Definition~\texttt{def:certificate} to \(m=1\).  Let \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  The first compatibility equation in Definition~\texttt{def:compatible-fiber} gives
\[
B=A^1=A.
\]
The second compatibility equation in that definition, together with \(A^0=I_d\), gives
\[
Q=\sum_{r=0}^{1-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top
  =A^0D(A^0)^\top
  =D.
\]
Therefore every member of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) equals \((B,Q)\), so the fiber has at most one member.

Conversely, substitute \((A,D)=(B,Q)\) into Definition~\texttt{def:compatible-fiber}.  The two coarse equations then hold identically, because \(B^1=B\) and \(B^0Q(B^0)^\top=Q\).  The remaining defining conditions hold if and only if
\[
B_{ij}=0\quad(i<j),
\qquad
B_{ij}=0\quad(i>j\ \text{and}\ j\to i\notin G),
\]
\[
\max_i|B_{ii}|<1,
\qquad
Q_{ij}=0\quad(i\ne j),
\qquad
Q\succ0.
\]
These are precisely the fine-grid compatibility constraints obtained by specializing that definition to \(m=1\).  Hence
\[
\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=
\begin{cases}
\{(B,Q)\},&\text{if all the displayed compatibility constraints hold},\\
\varnothing,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

It remains to verify the algorithmic output asserted in the proposition.  Under the same specialization, every diagonal root equation enumerated by \(\operatorname{Cert}_{uv,1,G}(B,Q)\) is
\[
a_{ii}^{,1}=B_{ii},
\]
and thus has the unique real solution \(a_{ii}=B_{ii}\).  By the declared definition of the divided-difference coefficient,
\[
C_1(x,y)=\sum_{r=0}^{0}x^r y^{0-r}=1.
\]
A nondecreasing walk of length one has at most one strict increase.  Consequently, the index set in the definition of the indirect-path remainder is empty and
\[
R_{vu,1}(A)=0.
\]
At each lower-triangular coordinate processed by the graph recursion in Definition~\texttt{def:certificate}, the root identity therefore reduces to
\[
B_{vu}=A_{vu}C_1(A_{vv},A_{uu})+R_{vu,1}(A)=A_{vu}.
\]
Thus every divided-difference coefficient is nonzero, the recursive enumeration has the unique transition candidate \(A=B\), and the coarse covariance equation has the unique innovation candidate \(D=Q\).  The exact compatibility test rejects this candidate exactly when one of the defining fiber constraints fails.  In that case the preceding fiber characterization gives \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=\varnothing\), so the certificate returns incompatibility.  Otherwise it accepts the unique compatible pair \((B,Q)\).

In the latter case, both copies in the certificate's two-copy transfer-inequality system must equal \((B,Q)\); hence that inequality system is infeasible.  The common-transfer branch consequently returns, using the declared definition of \(h_{uv}\),
\[
h_{uv}(z)
=\frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}
=\frac{B_{vu}z}{1-B_{vv}z}.
\]
Accepted compatibility also gives \(|B_{vv}|<1\).  Since \(z\in\mathbb T\) implies \(|z|=1\),
\[
|B_{vv}z|=|B_{vv}|<1,
\]
so \(1-B_{vv}z\ne0\).  The returned rational function is therefore well defined on \(\mathbb T\), and, because \(A=B\), it is exactly the unaliased direct fine-grid process transfer.  This proves every assertion of the proposition.
